findings.claim: check_hash_chain uses the wrong file paths for the no-fix-rounds case. When no fix-round subdirectories exist (highest == -1), the function looks for <slice-dir>/r1-correctness/dispatcher-result.json, r1-safety/dispatcher-result.json, and r1-completeness/dispatcher-result.json. These are the WP-level plan-review subdirectory conventions (as seen in docs/reviews/WP-SCP-022/r1-correctness/ etc.), not the per-slice dispatch artefact layout defined in §4.5, which places initial-round reviewer JSONs flat at review-{correctness,safety,completeness}.json. The gate will always emit exit 5 for any first-pass-approved slice because the expected files do not exist at those paths. The fix-round branch (highest >= 0) correctly uses review-{lens}.json relative to the terminal fix-round dir, confirming the flat naming is the per-slice dispatch convention.
findings.evidence: scripts/wp_scp_022_gate_check.sh lines 340–344: computed_corr=$(hash_file "$terminal_dir/r1-correctness/dispatcher-result.json" 2>/dev/null || true). §4.5 documents per-slice artefact layout as review-correctness.json, review-safety.json, review-completeness.json at the slice dispatch directory top-level for the initial round. Git status at conversation start shows docs/reviews/WP-SCP-022/r3-completeness/, r3-correctness/, r3-safety/ as the WP-plan-review directories — confirming r{N}-{lens}/ is the plan-review naming convention, not per-slice dispatch. Lines 346–348 (fix-round branch) look for review-correctness.json in terminal_dir, which is the §4.5 convention — proving the discrepancy is internal to the function.
findings.impact: The hash-chain gate is non-functional for every slice that achieves fixpoint on the first review pass. The orchestrator running --check-hash-chain <slice-id> before opening the slice PR always receives exit 5, blocking the autonomous chain and requiring manual intervention for every first-pass-approved slice. Operationally this creates pressure to skip or work around the check, undermining the invariant the check is meant to enforce. Additionally, an adversarial Codex executor who has write access to the dispatches directory (broader than normal implementation scope) could plant fabricated reviewer JSONs at r1-correctness/dispatcher-result.json while actual review files are at review-correctness.json, causing the gate to hash the fabricated copies while the real review result goes unverified.
findings.mitigation: Change the no-fix-rounds branch to match §4.5 convention: computed_corr=$(hash_file "$terminal_dir/review-correctness.json" 2>/dev/null || true), computed_safety=$(hash_file "$terminal_dir/review-safety.json" 2>/dev/null || true), computed_comp=$(hash_file "$terminal_dir/review-completeness.json" 2>/dev/null || true). Update the inline comment from 'reviewers landed at r1 directly' to 'initial round; artefacts at review-{lens}.json per §4.5'. Also add a sentence to §4.5 and §4.7 documenting the exact paths the orchestrator hashes when writing the sha256_chain block to fixpoint.md, removing all ambiguity between the plan-review directory convention and the per-slice dispatch convention.

findings.claim: verify_gate_commit_author() has two compounding defects that together make the signer-identity check both over-blocking (rejects the legitimate operator's work email) and over-permissive (accepts any email containing the configured string as a substring). First, the default SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL=jrnb2024 does not match the operator's configured email address james@brokai.net — gate artefacts committed from that identity fail the check despite being legitimate. Second, the third case alternative *"${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}"* is a substring match; any email containing jrnb2024 as a substring (e.g. impersonator-jrnb2024@attacker.example) passes. These are not independent: the configuration gap creates operational pressure to leave the env var unset, maximising exposure to the substring bypass.
findings.evidence: scripts/wp_scp_022_gate_check.sh line 51: SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL="${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL:-jrnb2024}". Line 108 case pattern: "${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}"|"${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}"@*|*"${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}"*. With default jrnb2024 and author email james@brokai.net: exact match jrnb2024 (no), prefix jrnb2024@* (no), substring *jrnb2024* (no — james@brokai.net does not contain the substring jrnb2024). Gate blocks the operator. Conversely, x-jrnb2024-spoof@attacker.example: substring *jrnb2024* (yes — passes). §8 R-022-12 states 'the orchestrator verifies the commit author is jrnb2024' but git log --format=%ae returns the author EMAIL, not the GitHub handle — confirming the default is a username being used as an email substring, not an email address. The env var SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL is settable by any process that runs the gate check, including subshells spawned during Codex dispatch if the check were ever called from within a dispatch context.
findings.impact: Every gate artefact committed by the operator via local git from james@brokai.net identity is rejected, forcing manual SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL override on every orchestrator invocation or breaking the autonomous chain silently. Any actor whose email contains the string jrnb2024 as a substring satisfies the identity check. The gate signer-identity defence introduced by R-022-12 to close R2-BYPASS-005 is substantially weaker than §8 documents: it provides at-best weak authorship attribution, not the authorised-identity enforcement described.
findings.mitigation: Change the default to the operator's actual primary git email: SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL="${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL:-james@brokai.net}". Add a second variable SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL_NOREPLY="${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL_NOREPLY:-jrnb2024@users.noreply.github.com}" for GitHub web-UI commits. Replace the three-alternative case with exact matches against both: "${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}"|"${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL_NOREPLY}". Remove the substring pattern *"${SCP_OPERATOR_EMAIL}"* entirely — exact and prefix-only matching is sufficient and eliminates the impersonation surface. Update §4.7 to document both accepted identities and the override procedure for rotating the operator email.

Schema violations in R2 result include missing_self_reported_concerns_defaulted_empty, confirming the field is expected and defaulted. §4.3 invariant 9 text in v0.3 plan: 'Free-text claim, evidence, impact, mitigation fields are passed through scripts/sanitize_review_finding.py' — self_reported_concerns is not named.
findings.impact: An adversarial reviewer can inject prompt-injection payloads via self_reported_concerns that bypass all sanitization: the full Unicode bypass set (U+2028/U+2029 closed in R2-BYPASS-003 for finding fields), backtick injection, and control-char injection all remain viable in this field. Exploitability depends on the Opus orchestrator's prompt assembly logic in ACC, which is not auditable from this repo. The risk is unguarded and unacknowledged.
findings.mitigation: Add explicit handling in §4.3 invariant 9: either (a) state that self_reported_concerns is DROPPED before fix-round prompt assembly and never passed to Codex, or (b) add a sanitize_review_result() function to sanitize_review_finding.py that applies sanitize_text() to each string in self_reported_concerns and to the top-level summary field before any orchestrator prompt assembly. Document the chosen approach in §4.3 so the ACC orchestrator has unambiguous guidance.

findings.claim: The R-022-13 rollback instruction for slice 020J is incomplete: the GitHub REST API endpoint for deleting a tag-protection rule requires the numeric rule ID returned by the creation call — DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags/protection/{tag_protection_id}. R-022-13 instructs Codex to 'invoke gh api -X DELETE to revert the successful call' without specifying that the tag_protection_id must be captured from the creation response and used in the rollback. Without the ID, the rollback call will fail (404 or hit a wrong endpoint), leaving the repo in the inconsistently-protected state R-022-13 is designed to prevent. The signed-commits rollback (DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/main/protection/required_signatures) requires no additional ID and is unaffected.
findings.evidence: WP-SCP-022 §8 R-022-13: 'on partial-apply (one OK, one error), Codex must invoke gh api -X DELETE to revert the successful call'. GitHub REST API for tag protection: POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags/protection returns {id: integer, ...}; DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags/protection/{tag_protection_id} requires the numeric id as path parameter. Without it, gh api -X DELETE repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags/protection would fail or return a listing. R-022-13 does not instruct Codex to capture or preserve the creation response id. 020J is PRECONDITION for 020D1 — an incorrectly-rolled-back 020J leaves the v* tag rule active but unsigned-commits permitted, breaking the §8 bootstrap-trust invariant.
findings.mitigation: Amend R-022-13: the 020J dispatch package instruction must explicitly tell Codex to (1) parse the tag_protection_id integer from the POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags/protection response body, (2) on partial-apply, invoke gh api -X DELETE repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags/protection/${tag_protection_id} with the captured ID, (3) verify the rollback succeeded by querying GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags/protection and asserting an empty array before reporting status=blocked. The plan text 'invoke gh api -X DELETE' should be replaced with the fully-specified endpoint including the ID preservation step.

findings.claim: R2-BYPASS-007 carry-forward: docs/reviews/WP-SCP-022/acc-pin-manifest.json still has no CODEOWNERS entry and no hardcoded integrity hash in the gate script. v0.3 closes R2 C-R2-005 (silent skip when jq missing) but does not implement the structural CODEOWNERS protection or manifest hash-anchor recommended in R2-BYPASS-007's mitigation.
findings.evidence: scripts/wp_scp_022_gate_check.sh check_acc_pin() reads the manifest at line 245 (jq -r '.acc_repo_head' "$PIN_MANIFEST") with no prior integrity check. No CODEOWNERS entry for docs/reviews/WP-SCP-022/acc-pin-manifest.json is mentioned in v0.3 plan §4.7 or the plan AC in §9. R2-BYPASS-007 mitigation recommended both a CODEOWNERS entry and a hardcoded SHA-256 manifest hash in the gate script verified before parsing.
findings.mitigation: Add docs/reviews/WP-SCP-022/acc-pin-manifest.json @jrnb2024 to CODEOWNERS. Optionally prepend an EXPECTED_MANIFEST_SHA256 constant in wp_scp_022_gate_check.sh and assert sha256sum/shasum of the manifest matches before parsing its contents.

self_reported_concerns: R3-BYPASS-001 and R3-BYPASS-002 together mean the autonomous chain cannot successfully complete any gate-check cycle for first-pass-approved slices committed from the operator's local git identity without manual env-var overrides or script edits. Both must be fixed before the first implementation slice is dispatched or the gate enforcement machinery will fail on its first operational use.
structured_review.summary: v0.3 cleanly closes 4 R2 findings (R2-BYPASS-002 id sanitization, R2-BYPASS-003 Unicode separators, R2-BYPASS-004 readlink portability, R2-BYPASS-008 git-repo guard) and adds R-022-13 for 020J partial-apply rollback with accepted residual. Two R2 findings are only partially addressed and produce new MAJ findings: check_hash_chain uses wrong file paths for the no-fix-rounds case making the gate permanently non-functional for first-pass-approved slices (R3-BYPASS-001 MAJ), and the signer-identity check uses an over-broad substring pattern with a default that does not match the operator's actual email james@brokai.net (R3-BYPASS-002 MAJ). Three further findings: self_reported_concerns is outside sanitization scope (R3-BYPASS-003 MIN), 020J tag-protection rollback instruction omits the required rule ID (R3-BYPASS-004 MIN), and R2-BYPASS-007 CODEOWNERS recommendation remains unimplemented (R3-BYPASS-005 nit). Verdict: CHANGES_REQUESTED on 2 MAJ findings.
